# Summaries and tables

## `summarise()` example

## `gtsummary` example

Using the `gtsummary` package

```{r}
library(gtsummary)
```

## `gtsummary` example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
penguin_summary <- tbl_summary(
  data,
  by = species,    # <1>
  include = c(     # <2>
    sex,           # <2>
    bill_len,      # <2>
    flipper_len,   # <2>
    sex            # <2>
  )                # <2>
)
```

1. Which variable to produce summaries by
2. Which variables to summarise

:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: false
library(gt)
penguin_summary |> 
  as_gt() |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(30),
    table.margin.left = px(10)
  )
```

:::
::::

```{r}
penguin_summary <- tbl_summary(
  data,
    by = species, # <1>
  include = c( # <2>
    sex, # <2>
    bill_len, # <2>
    flipper_len, # <2>
    sex # <2>
  ), # <2>
  statistic = list( # <3>
```

```{r}
    sex = "Sex", # <4>
    bill_len = "Bill length", # <4>
    flipper_len = "Flipper length", # <4>
```

```{r}
  ), # <4>

)
```

## `gtsummary` example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

To save the output from `gtsummary`, we:

- convert it to a `tibble`
- save this as `csv` file

```{r}
penguin_summary |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  write_csv(
    "data/penguin_summary.csv",
    na = ""
    )
```

## Other packages to consider

Summarising data:

- `janitor` has the `tabyl()` function
- `dplyr` has the `summarise()` function

Creating tables via Quarto or RMarkdown:

- `flextable` has the best MS Word support
- `kable` is good for PDF output
- `gt` is highly customisable for HTML output

# Data visualisation

## Package options

`plot()` — base R

`ggplot2` — part of the `tidyverse`, highly customisable

`tidyplots` — simpler interface to `ggplot2`

## `ggplot2`

All plots start with the `ggplot()` function

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len
  )
)
```

## Scatter plot

From this, we add to the plot using the `+` symbol

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len
  )
) +
  geom_point()
```

## Bar plot

For some plots, it doesn't make sense to plot the raw data.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species,
    y = body_mass
  )
) +
  geom_col()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Use `geom_col()` on summarised data, `geom_bar()` to summarise raw data
:::

## Bar plot

Instead, we need to summarise the data first and plot the summarised values

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = T),
    .by = species
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = species,
      y = mean_body_mass
    )
  ) +
  geom_col()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Use `geom_col()` on summarised data, `geom_bar()` to summarise raw data
:::

## Line graph

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = body_mass
  )
) +
geom_line()
```

## Line graph

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = T),
    .by = c(year, species)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = mean_body_mass,
      colour = species
    )
  ) +
  geom_line()
```

## Customising a plot

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    shape = 1
    )

penguin_plot
```

## Customising axes

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Flipper length (mm)",
    limits = c(160, 240),
    breaks = seq(160,240,20),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Bill length (mm)",
    limits = c(30, 60),
    breaks = seq(30, 60, 10),
    minor_breaks = seq(35, 55, 10)
  ) 
penguin_plot
```

## Customising the legend

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot + 
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Species",
    values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 6)))
penguin_plot
```

## Customising with a theme

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot + 
  theme_bw(
    base_size = 25,
    base_family = "serif"
  )
penguin_plot
```

::: {.callout-tip}
There are several themes available! `theme_minimal()` is popular, but has a transparent background.
:::

## Adding an element

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    linetype = "dashed",
    show.legend = FALSE
  )
penguin_plot
```

## Adding a facet

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  facet_wrap(~ sex)
penguin_plot
```

## Saving the output

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

```{r}
ggsave(
  "img/penguin_plot.png",
  penguin_plot,
  width = 16,
  height = 9,
  units = "in",
)
```

## Let's practice!

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="65%"}

Use `ggplot2` to make a bar chart showing the count of each penguin species, format the axes, and add a theme.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Initial specification"
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Adding the bars"
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species
  )
) +
  geom_bar()
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Format the axes"
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species
  )
) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Count",
    limits = c(0, 160)
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Add a theme"
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species
  )
) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Count",
    limits = c(0, 160)
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Regression

## Model notation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
To regress `body_mass` on `sex` and `species`, we write:

```{r}
regression_results <- lm(
  body_mass ~ sex + species,
  data = data
)
```

- Outcome (`body_mass`) left of the tilde `~`
- Covariates right of the tilde, separated with a plus `+`

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
lm(
  formula, 
  data, 
  subset, 
  weights, 
  na.action,
  method = "qr",
  model = TRUE, 
  x = FALSE, 
  y = FALSE, 
  qr = TRUE,
  singular.ok = TRUE,
  contrasts = NULL,
  offset, 
  ...,
  digits
  )
```

:::
::::

## Available models*

Base R

- Linear `lm()`
- Generalised linear `glm()`
  - Binomial
  - Poisson
  

Packages for common models:

- `lme4`
- `gee`
- `glmm`
- `brms`
